concepts.title: Approximation Error
concepts.one_liner: Approximation error is the total cost incurred on the training data set, representing the gap between the model and the training data points.
concepts.content:
Approximation error is the gap between the model line and the training data points. Let $\{x_{(\texttt{train})}^{(i)}, y_{(\texttt{train})}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^N$ be our training data set. Then the approximation error $J_{\texttt{approx}}$ is defined as the total cost incurred on this training data:

$$\begin{aligned}
    J_{\texttt{approx}} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \mathcal{L}(f_{\theta}(x_{(\texttt{train})}^{(i)}), y_{(\texttt{train})}^{(i)})
\end{aligned}$$

Notice that approximation error is the cost function we minimize in empirical risk minimization.
concepts.motivation_md: In machine learning, we need a way to measure how well our model fits the data we currently have. Approximation error provides this metric, serving as the objective function that we minimize during the training process to ensure the model captures the patterns in the training set.
concepts.recap_md: - It measures the discrepancy between the model's predictions and the actual training data points.

concepts.title: Generalization Error
concepts.one_liner: Generalization error is the expected cost incurred when sampling a new test point at random from the true data generating process.
concepts.content:
Generalization error is the expected cost we would incur if we sampled a new test point at random from the true data generating process. It is often approximated by measuring performance on a heldout validation set, $\{x_{(\texttt{val})}^{(i)}, y_{(\texttt{val})}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^N$, which can simply be a subset of the data that we don't use for training or testing:

$$\begin{aligned}
    J_{\texttt{gen}} &= \mathbb{E}_{x,y \sim p_{\texttt{data}}} [ \mathcal{L}(f_{\theta}(x), y)]\\
                        &\approx \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \mathcal{L}(f_{\theta}(x_{(\texttt{val})}^{(i)}), y_{(\texttt{val})}^{(i)})
\end{aligned}$$
concepts.motivation_md: The ultimate goal of a machine learning model is to perform well on unseen data, not just the training set. Generalization error quantifies this performance, helping us detect if a model has simply memorized the training data rather than learning the underlying patterns.
concepts.recap_md: - It represents the expected loss over the true data distribution $p_{\texttt{data}}$.

concepts.title: U-shaped Generalization Curve
concepts.one_liner: Generalization error typically follows a U-shaped curve relative to model complexity, starting high due to underfitting and rising again due to overfitting.
concepts.content:
Approximation error goes down with increasing $K$ but all we really care about is generalization error, which measures how well we will do on test queries that are newly sampled from the true data generating process. For polynomial regression, generalization error obeys a U-shaped function with respect to $K$: at first it is high because we are underfitting; gradually we fit the data better and better and eventually we overfit, with generalization error becoming high again.

concepts.title: Regularization
concepts.one_liner: Regularization refers to mechanisms that penalize function complexity to avoid learning overly flexible functions that overfit the data.
concepts.motivation_md: To prevent models from becoming too complex and fitting noise in the training data, we need a way to constrain them. Regularization provides a mathematical framework to balance fitting the data well against keeping the model simple.
concepts.recap_md: - It adds a penalty term $R(\theta)$ to the loss function to discourage complexity.

slots.motivation: To prevent models from becoming too complex and fitting noise in the training data, we need a way to constrain them. Regularization provides a mathematical framework to balance fitting the data well against keeping the model simple.
slots.key_passage: - It adds a penalty term $R(\theta)$ to the loss function to discourage complexity.

concepts.title: Occam's Razor
concepts.one_liner: Occam's razor is the principle that when multiple functions can explain the data, the simplest one should be preferred.
concepts.content: Occam's razor is a principle embodied by regularization: when multiple functions can explain the data, give preference to the simplest. In the context of learning, this means preferring hypotheses that are sufficiently expressive to fit the data but not so flexible that they overfit. For example, we might prefer a linear function over a quadratic one if both explain the observations sufficiently well.
concepts.motivation_md: In machine learning, there are often infinitely many functions that can fit a finite set of data points. Occam's razor provides a philosophical and practical heuristic for choosing the function most likely to generalize to new data.
concepts.recap_md: - It suggests that simpler explanations are generally better than complex ones.

concepts.title: Lp Norm Regularization
concepts.one_liner: Lp norm regularization penalizes the parameters of a model using the $L_p$ norm to control complexity.
concepts.content:
One of the most common regularizers is to penalize the $L_p$ norm of the parameters of our model, $\theta$:
$$
R(\theta) = \left\lVert\theta\right\rVert_{p}.
$$
The $L_p$-norm of $\mathbf{x}$ is defined as $(\sum_i |x_i|^{p})^{\frac{1}{p}}$. For example, the $L_2$-norm corresponds to the familiar least-squares objective.
concepts.motivation_md: We need a concrete mathematical way to measure 'complexity' in terms of model parameters. Using the magnitude of the parameter vector (the norm) is an effective proxy for complexity, as smaller weights often lead to simpler, smoother functions.
concepts.recap_md: - It uses the $L_p$ norm $(\sum_i |x_i|^{p})^{\frac{1}{p}}$ as a penalty term.

concepts.title: Ridge Regression (Tikonov Regression)
concepts.one_liner: Ridge regression is a form of regularized regression that uses an $L_2$ norm penalty on the model parameters.
concepts.content: Ridge regression, also known as Tikonov regression, is a common regularization technique where the $L_p$ norm penalty is applied with $p=2$.
concepts.motivation_md: Ridge regression is used to prevent overfitting and handle multicollinearity in regression models by shrinking the coefficients toward zero, though not exactly to zero.
concepts.recap_md: - It corresponds to $L_p$ norm regularization with $p=2$.

concepts.title: Lasso Regression
concepts.one_liner: Lasso regression is a form of regularized regression that uses an $L_1$ norm penalty on the model parameters.
concepts.content: Lasso regression is the name given to regression problems that apply an $L_p$ regularizer with $p=1$.
concepts.motivation_md: Lasso is particularly useful when we suspect that many input features are irrelevant, as the $L_1$ penalty tends to produce sparse solutions where some coefficients are exactly zero.
concepts.recap_md: - It corresponds to $L_p$ norm regularization with $p=1$.

concepts.title: Hard vs Soft Constraints in Learning

position.section_title: Three Tools in the Search for Truth: Data, Priors, and Hypotheses

concepts.one_liner: The hypothesis space places hard constraints on search that cannot be violated, while data and priors apply soft constraints that incur a penalty when violated.
concepts.content: The hypothesis space places hard constraints on our search; we cannot violate them. Data and priors apply soft constraints; we can violate them but we will pay a penalty.
concepts.motivation_md: In machine learning, it is important to distinguish between what the model is fundamentally capable of representing (hard constraints) and what the model is encouraged to prefer based on evidence (soft constraints).
concepts.recap_md:
- Hard constraints are defined by the hypothesis space and cannot be violated.
- Soft constraints are derived from data and priors and can be violated at the cost of a penalty.

concepts.title: Generalization in Learning
concepts.one_liner: The goal of learning is to extract lessons from past data that allow systems to continue working even when test data differs from training data.
concepts.content: The goal of learning is to extract lessons from past data to help on future problem solving. Unless the future is identical to the past, this is a problem that requires generalization. One goal of learning algorithms is to make systems that generalize ever better, meaning they continue to work even when the test data is very different than the training data. Currently, however, the systems that generalize in the strongest sense—that work for all possible test data—are generally not learned but designed according to other principles. In this way, many classical algorithms still have advantages over the latest learned systems. But this gap is rapidly closing!
concepts.motivation_md: Learning is only useful if it applies to new, unseen situations. Generalization is the metric for how well a model has captured underlying patterns rather than just memorizing specific examples.
concepts.recap_md:
- Generalization allows a system to perform correctly on test data that differs from training data.
- Strong generalization for all possible data is often a feature of designed rather than learned algorithms.
- The gap between classical designed algorithms and learned systems is narrowing.

concepts.title: Overfitting
concepts.one_liner: Overfitting occurs when a model fits properties in the training data that do not exist in the test data, leading to high training performance but low test performance.
concepts.content: Learning theory studies the settings under which optimization on the training set yields good results on the test set. In general it may not, since the test set may have different properties from the training set. When we fit to properties in the training data that do not exist in the test data, we call this overfitting. When this happens, training performance will be high, but test performance can be very low, since what we learned about the training data does not generalize to the test data.
concepts.motivation_md: Overfitting is a central challenge in machine learning where a model becomes too specialized to its training examples, losing its ability to make accurate predictions on new, unseen data.
concepts.recap_md: - Overfitting happens when a model captures noise or specific training set quirks instead of the underlying relationship.

concepts.title: Generalization
concepts.one_liner: Generalization is the ability of a model to apply what it learned from training data to perform well on unseen test data.
concepts.content: Learning theory studies the settings under which optimization on the training set yields good results on the test set. When this happens, training performance will be high, but test performance can be very low, since what we learned about the training data does not generalize to the test data.
concepts.motivation_md: The ultimate goal of machine learning is not just to memorize training data, but to generalize—to perform accurately on new data the model has never encountered before.
concepts.recap_md: - Generalization refers to how well a model's learned patterns apply to a separate test set.

concepts.title: Underfitting
concepts.one_liner: Underfitting occurs when a learner fails to optimize the objective on the training data.
concepts.content: A learner may perform poorly for one of two reasons: either it failed to optimize the objective on the training data, or it succeeded on the training data but in a way that does not generalize to the test setting. The former is called underfitting and the latter is called overfitting.
concepts.motivation_md: Underfitting identifies when a model is too simple or training has not progressed enough to capture the basic patterns in the data.
concepts.recap_md: - Underfitting is characterized by poor performance even on the training data itself.

concepts.title: Polynomial Regression
concepts.one_liner: Polynomial regression is a learning problem where the hypothesis space consists of polynomial functions of a specified degree $K$.
concepts.content: Polynomial regression is just like linear regression except that the hypothesis space is polynomial functions rather than linear functions, that is, $$y = f_{\theta}(x) = \sum_{k=0}^K \theta_k x^k$$ where $K$, the degree of the polynomial, is a hyperparameter of the hypothesis space. In the setting where we use the least-squares ($L_2$) loss function, polynomial regression is highly related to linear regression; in fact, we can transform a polynomial regression problem into a linear regression problem.
concepts.motivation_md: Linear models are often too simple to capture curved relationships in data. Polynomial regression allows for more flexible curves while still benefiting from the well-understood optimization techniques of linear regression.
concepts.recap_md: - Polynomial regression uses a hypothesis space of the form $f_{\theta}(x) = \sum_{k=0}^K \theta_k x^k$.

slots.key_passage: - Polynomial regression uses a hypothesis space of the form $f_{\theta}(x) = \sum_{k=0}^K \theta_k x^k$.

In the setting where we use the least-squares ($L_2$) loss function, polynomial regression is highly related to linear regression; in fact, we can transform a polynomial regression problem into a linear regression problem.

concepts.title: Polynomial Regression as Linear Regression
concepts.one_liner: Polynomial regression can be treated as a linear regression problem by featurizing the input $x$ into a vector of its powers.
concepts.content: We can rewrite a polynomial as a linear function in the parameters $\theta$: $$\sum_{k=0}^K \theta_k x^k = \theta^\mathsf{T}\phi(x)$$ where $$\phi(x) = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ x \\ x^2 \\ \vdots \\ x^K \end{bmatrix}$$. By featurizing $x$ and representing each datapoint with the feature vector $\phi(x)$, we arrive at a linear regression problem in this feature space. The learning problem and closed-form optimizer for $L_2$ polynomial regression are almost identical to $L_2$ linear regression, using a data matrix $\mathbf{\Phi}$: $$\mathbf{\Phi} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & x^{(1)} & x^{(1)^2} & ... & x^{(1)^K} \\ 1 & x^{(2)} & x^{(2)^2} & ... & x^{(2)^K} \\ \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots \\ 1 & x^{(N)} & x^{(N)^2} & ... & x^{(N)^K} \end{bmatrix}$$. The matrix $\mathbf{\Phi}$ is an array of the features (columns) for each datapoint (rows).
concepts.motivation_md: This technique allows us to solve non-linear problems using the powerful and efficient tools developed for linear regression, simply by changing how we represent the input data.
concepts.recap_md: - Featurizing $x$ into $\phi(x)$ makes the polynomial function linear with respect to the parameters $\theta$.

concepts.title: Data Generating Process
concepts.one_liner: The data generating process is the full process, including the true underlying relationship and observation noise, that produces observed data.
concepts.content: The observed data $\{x^{(i)}, y^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^N$ is sampled from a ground truth relationship plus observation noise. We refer to the full process that generates the data as the data generating process. For example, if the true relationship is $Y = X^2 + 1$ and the observation noise is $\epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1)$, then the noisy observations $Y^\prime = Y + \epsilon$ and the resulting samples $x,y \sim p(X,Y^{\prime})$ constitute the data-generating process.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding the data generating process helps distinguish between the actual signal we want to learn and the random noise that we should ignore.
concepts.recap_md: - The data generating process combines a true underlying relationship with random observation noise.

concepts.title: Weight Decay
concepts.one_liner: In the context of neural networks, weight decay is a regularizer that penalizes the size of the parameters.
concepts.content: In the context of neural networks, this regularizer is called weight decay. When $p=1$, the regularizer is based on the $L_1$ norm.
concepts.motivation_md: Weight decay is used to prevent overfitting in neural networks by penalizing large parameter values, effectively encouraging the model to find simpler solutions that generalize better.
concepts.recap_md: - Weight decay is a common term for parameter regularization in neural networks.

concepts.title: Regularizers as Probabilistic Priors
concepts.one_liner: Regularizers can be interpreted as probabilistic priors that prefer certain solutions over others before looking at the data.
concepts.content: Regularizers can be interpreted as priors that prefer, a priori (before looking at the data), some solutions over others. Under this interpretation, the data fit loss (e.g., $L_2$ loss) is a likelihood function $p(\{y^{(i)}\}^N_{i=1} \bigm | \{x^{(i)}\}^N_{i=1}, \theta)$ and the regularizer is a prior $p(\theta)$. Bayes' rule then states that the posterior $p(\theta \bigm | \{x^{(i)}, y^{(i)}\}^N_{i=1})$ is proportional to the product of the prior and the likelihood. The log posterior is then the sum of the log likelihood and the log prior, plus a constant. Hence we arrive at the form of a regularized objective function.
concepts.motivation_md: This perspective provides a formal statistical foundation for regularization, allowing us to use Bayesian inference to justify why we add penalty terms to our loss functions.
concepts.recap_md: - Regularizers act as a prior probability distribution $p(\theta)$ over the model parameters.

slots.motivation: This perspective provides a formal statistical foundation for regularization, allowing us to use Bayesian inference to justify why we add penalty terms to our loss functions.
slots.key_passage: - Regularizers act as a prior probability distribution $p(\theta)$ over the model parameters.

concepts.title: Bayesian Occam's Razor
concepts.one_liner: The Bayesian Occam's razor suggests that simpler hypotheses are more likely because complex hypothesis spaces must spread their prior probability mass more thinly.
concepts.content: These priors are not arbitrarily chosen. The notion of the Bayesian Occam's razor derives such priors by noting that more complex hypothesis spaces must cover more possible hypotheses, and therefore must assign less prior mass to any single hypothesis. This is because the prior probability of all possible hypotheses in the hypothesis space must sum to 1. This is why, probabilistically, simpler hypotheses are more likely to be true.
concepts.motivation_md: It provides a mathematical justification for the principle of parsimony, explaining why we should prefer simpler models unless the data strongly supports a complex one.
concepts.recap_md: - Complex models assign less prior probability to any single hypothesis because they cover a larger space.

concepts.title: Model Capacity
concepts.one_liner: Model capacity refers to the expressivity of a hypothesis space, for which the number of parameters is only a rough proxy.
concepts.content: A recent empirical finding is that some seemingly complex hypothesis spaces, such as deep nets, tend not to overfit, even though they have many more free parameters than the number of datapoints they are fit to. The number of parameters is just a rough proxy for model capacity (i.e., the expressivity of the hypothesis space). A single parameter that has infinite numerical precision can parameterize an arbitrarily complex function, defining a very expressive hypothesis space capable of overfitting. Conversely, if we have a million parameters that are regularized so that almost all are zero, they may define a simple class of functions which does not overfit. While the number of parameters is a rough estimate of model capacity, it is not the full story.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding capacity helps explain why large models like neural networks can sometimes generalize well despite having millions of parameters, and why regularization is essential.
concepts.recap_md: - Model capacity measures the expressivity of the hypothesis space.

concepts.title: Three Tools for Generalization: Data, Priors, and Hypotheses

position.section_title: Three Tools in the Search for Truth: Data, Priors, and Hypotheses

concepts.one_liner: Learning and generalization can be viewed as a search for truth using three primary tools: data, priors, and the hypothesis space.
concepts.content:
Learning can be considered as akin to searching for a needle (the "truth" or true function) in a haystack (the hypothesis space). We have three tools to pinpoint this location:

1. Data: Observations of the world that provide explanations consistent with observed facts.
2. Priors: Also known as regularizers, these prefer some solutions over others a priori.
3. Hypotheses: The set of functions under consideration. The hypothesis space $\mathcal{F}$ constrains which solutions we can possibly find; if the truth is not in our space, no amount of data can find it.

Together these three tools allow us to pinpoint good solutions in the space of all possibilities.

(see figure: A cartoon of the tools for honing in on the truth.)

In this framework, the hypothesis space $\mathcal{F}$ (white circle) places a hard constraint, the prior (yellow ellipse) places a soft constraint on preferred mappings, and the data (green ellipse) places a soft constraint preferring mappings that fit the observations. While approximation error is low in the data-fitting region, we bias our picks toward the prior region to improve generalization. A learning algorithm searches over $\mathcal{F}$ to maximize the likelihood times the prior.
concepts.motivation_md: This framework helps conceptualize how different components of machine learning—the model architecture, the loss function, and the dataset—interact to find a generalizable solution.
concepts.recap_md: - Data, priors, and hypothesis spaces act as constraints to narrow down the search for the true function.

concepts.title: Effect of Priors on Learning

position.section_title: Three Tools in the Search for Truth: Data, Priors, and Hypotheses

concepts.one_liner: Priors act as soft constraints that pull learned solutions toward preferred regions of the parameter space, such as the origin.
concepts.content:
The effect of priors can be observed using an objective function like $J(\theta; \{x^{(i)}, y^{(i)}\}^N_{i=1}) = \frac{1}{N}\sum_i \left\lVert f_{\theta}(x^{(i)}) - y^{(i)}\right\rVert_2^2 + \lambda \left\lVert\theta\right\rVert_2^2$ with a linear hypothesis space $f_{\theta}(x) = \theta_0 + \theta_1 x$. The ridge regularizer $\left\lVert\theta\right\rVert_2^2$ prefers solutions with small parameter norms, placing a quadratic bowl around the origin in the energy landscape. As the regularization strength $\lambda$ increases, the solution is pulled closer to the origin.

(see figure: More regularization, more (soft) constraints.)

Lessons from this effect include:
1. Priors help only when they are good guesses as to the truth.
2. Overreliance on the prior means ignoring the data, which is generally detrimental.
3. There is an optimal "sweet spot" for the strength of any given prior.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding the effect of priors allows practitioners to balance the trade-off between fitting the training data and adhering to pre-existing beliefs about the model parameters.
concepts.recap_md: - Priors pull the learned solution toward a preferred region, such as small parameter values.

concepts.title: Ridge Regularization

position.section_title: Three Tools in the Search for Truth: Data, Priors, and Hypotheses

concepts.one_liner: Ridge regularization adds a penalty proportional to the squared norm of the parameters to the objective function.
concepts.content:
The ridge regularizer $\left\lVert\theta\right\rVert_2^2$ prefers solutions with small parameter norms. Its contribution to the energy landscape is to place a quadratic bowl around the origin. As the regularization parameter $\lambda$ increases, the effect of the regularizer becomes stronger and pulls the learned solution closer and closer to the origin.

(see figure: More regularization, more (soft) constraints.)
concepts.motivation_md: Ridge regularization is a standard technique to prevent overfitting by discouraging large weights, which often leads to more stable and generalizable models.
concepts.recap_md: - Ridge regularization uses the squared $L_2$ norm of parameters as a penalty.

concepts.title: Effect of Hypothesis Space on Learning

position.section_title: Three Tools in the Search for Truth: Data, Priors, and Hypotheses

concepts.one_liner: The choice of hypothesis space acts as a hard constraint on learning, where smaller spaces can accelerate search but may exclude the true solution.
concepts.content:
The hypothesis space itself acts as a tool for learning. Consider three spaces: quadratic ($f_{\theta}(x) = \theta_0 x + \theta_1 x^2$), linear ($f_{\theta}(x) = \theta_0 x$), and constant ($f_{\theta}(x) = 0$).

(see figure: Fewer hypotheses, more (hard) constraints)

If the true function is linear, both the quadratic and linear spaces contain the truth. However, the linear space is much smaller, allowing the learning process to ignore large regions of parameter space (e.g., where $\theta_1 \neq 0$), which can accelerate the search. Conversely, a space can be too small; the constant hypothesis space makes search trivial but fails if the truth is not a constant zero function.
concepts.motivation_md: Choosing the right hypothesis space is a fundamental trade-off: a larger space is more likely to contain the truth but is harder to search and prone to overfitting, while a smaller space is easier to optimize but may suffer from bias.
concepts.recap_md: - Smaller hypothesis spaces provide hard constraints that can speed up learning.

Generalization error is defined as the expected cost when sampling new points from the true data generating process.
The curve describes the specific behavior of generalization error as model complexity changes.
The initial high error in the U-shaped curve is attributed to underfitting.
The eventual rise in the U-shaped curve is attributed to the model overfitting the data.
Regularization is specifically introduced as a mechanism to avoid learning overly flexible functions that overfit the data.
Lp norm regularization is a specific technique for implementing the general concept of regularization.
Weight decay is the term used for parameter norm regularization in the specific context of neural networks.
The Bayesian justification for simplicity relies on the distribution of prior probability mass across hypothesis spaces.
The concept of generalization in learning is built directly upon the fundamental definition of generalization as performance on unseen data.
The discussion of designed versus learned systems for generalization relies on the previously established tools of data, priors, and hypotheses.
The tools are presented as the means to achieve the goal of generalization in learning.
Priors, the second tool for generalization, are identified as regularizers.
This concept explores the specific impact of one of the three tools (priors) introduced in the generalization framework.
The effect of priors is demonstrated concretely using the ridge regularizer as a specific example.
This concept explores the specific impact of the third tool (hypothesis space) introduced in the generalization framework.
The definition of soft constraints relies on the understanding of how priors and data function as penalties.
The definition of hard constraints relies on the understanding of how the hypothesis space limits the search area.

overlay.rationale: Underfitting and overfitting are the two primary reasons a learner may perform poorly, representing failures in optimization versus generalization.
Approximation error measures performance on training data, while generalization error measures expected performance on new samples.
Polynomial regression of varying degrees K serves as the primary example for demonstrating the U-shaped generalization curve.
Generalization is the success case of learning, whereas overfitting represents the failure to generalize by fitting training-specific noise.
Regularization is a mathematical embodiment of the principle of Occam's razor, preferring simpler functions.
Ridge regression is defined as the specific case of Lp norm regularization where p=2.
Lasso regression is defined as the specific case of Lp norm regularization where p=1.
The probabilistic interpretation provides a formal Bayesian framework for why we add regularizers to objective functions.
Bayesian Occam's razor provides a probabilistic derivation and justification for the general Occam's razor principle.
Generalization is the ultimate goal of learning, whereas overfitting represents the failure to generalize by being too tied to specific past data.
The text demonstrates how a regularizer (ridge) acts as a prior by pulling solutions toward a preferred region (the origin).
Ridge regularization is a specific instance of Lp norm regularization where p=2.
Ridge regularization is the penalty component that defines ridge regression.
The comparison between quadratic, linear, and constant spaces illustrates how the size (capacity) of the hypothesis space affects learning.
Model capacity is a central concept used to explain why and when models overfit, particularly in the context of parameter count.
Regularization is used to demonstrate that the number of parameters is not the sole determinant of a model's effective capacity.
